docs.t: Judge Brian Charles Lea (W.D. Tenn.) — Conferences
docs.x: Judge Brian Charles Lea, W.D. Tenn.. Conferences: Scheduling, status, and similar case-management conferences are by default on Microsoft Teams video. To have one in person, file a motion at least 7 days before; the court may also set one in person on its own.

docs.t: Judge Brian Charles Lea (W.D. Tenn.) — Discovery and experts
docs.x: Judge Brian Charles Lea, W.D. Tenn.. Discovery and experts: Serve written discovery early enough that responses are due before the deadline. Parties may agree to discovery after a deadline, but the court won’t take up disputes arising after it absent exceptional circumstances. Confer and comply with L.R. 26.1 before raising disputes. Motions to compel are due within 45 days of the default or response at issue, or within 30 days if it occurs within 30 days of the discovery deadline. No depositions after the discovery deadline. Don’t file expert reports generally, but a movant to exclude an expert must file the report with the motion, and any party relying on a report for a motion or opposition must file it.

docs.t: Judge Brian Charles Lea (W.D. Tenn.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Brian Charles Lea, W.D. Tenn.. Sealing: Agreed confidentiality terms do not justify sealing. Move for leave under the Local Rules, guided by Rule 26(c) and Procter & Gamble Co. v. Bankers Trust Co., 78 F.3d 219 (6th Cir. 1996); such motions are closely scrutinized.

docs.t: Judge Brian Charles Lea (W.D. Tenn.) — Scheduling-order tracks
docs.x: Judge Brian Charles Lea, W.D. Tenn.. Expedited track (no scheduling conference): discovery closes 180 days after service, with experts at 30/20/10 days before close. Complex track dates are set case by case, with motions in limine at least 4 months after the dispositive-motion deadline. Plaintiff’s counsel initiates, but all counsel are responsible. docs.t: Judge Brian Charles Lea (W.D. Tenn.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian Charles Lea, W.D. Tenn.. Trial (trap): The court conducts voir dire; special questions go to the ECF Inbox in Word at least 2 weeks before trial. No argument in openings (closing time may be cut for violations). Visual media in openings or closings only if admitted or stipulated; otherwise move in advance. Stand to address the court or object; only one attorney per witness. Move exhibits in individually, around when presented, unless stipulated. Jurors may take notes and get written instructions. During deliberations, counsel who leave must tell the deputy where they are and be able to return within 10 minutes. The judge conducts any jury polling.

If that exchange does not settle the case, each side delivers an in camera statement to ECF_Judge_Claxton@tnwd.uscourts.gov no later than 3 business days before the conference: facts, strengths and weaknesses, and copies of the demand and offer. docs.x: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton, W.D. Tenn.. Model scheduling order for routine cases: The judge’s model sets joinder and amendment motions within 2 months after the conference, motions to dismiss within 3 months, discovery within 6 to 8 months, plaintiff’s expert disclosures 2 months and defendant’s 1 month before the close of discovery, and Daubert and dispositive motions within 1 month after it. The model requires motions to compel by the discovery deadline or within 30 days of the default or response if it occurs within 30 days of that deadline; the newer district track templates on the same page use 45 days. The pretrial and trial dates are set by the presiding judge. The page links the district’s Local Rule 16.2 Standard, Expedited, and Complex Track scheduling-order templates (identical on every judge’s page). docs.t: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton (W.D. Tenn.) — Exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton, W.D. Tenn.. Exhibits (trap): Exchange an A list (will introduce) and a B list (may introduce) of exhibits 10 days before trial. Number all exhibits consecutively, preferably A-list exhibits first. At the start of trial, give the courtroom deputy the original A-list exhibits with colored tags (plaintiff blue, defendant yellow) stapled to the upper right corner of the first page, plus an exhibit list with the ID, Admitted, Witness, and Objection columns left blank. Also provide two bench books of A-list copies (judge and witness box), tabbed with number tabs; the judge’s book must include an exhibit list showing any objections. Unobjected-to A-list exhibits are admitted at the outset of the presenting party’s case.

docs.t: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton (W.D. Tenn.) — Deposition designations
docs.x: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton, W.D. Tenn.. Deposition designations: At least five days before trial, e-file a single color-coded copy of each deposition transcript showing each party’s designations in different highlight colors, with objections noted in the margin, and give the court a paper copy. Use full-page format.

docs.t: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton (W.D. Tenn.) — Witnesses, voir dire, and trial day
docs.x: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton, W.D. Tenn.. Witnesses, voir dire, and trial day: Exchange A (will call) and B (might call) witness lists 10 days before trial. By the end of each day, the presenting party must tell the other side and the court which witnesses it will call the next day. The court conducts voir dire, considering the parties’ proposed questions, then asks counsel for any additional questions. Court normally sits 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. with 1 hour and 15 minutes for lunch. Dress appropriately; no food in the courtroom (bottled water is allowed). Counsel are encouraged to follow the American College of Trial Lawyers’ Codes of Pretrial and Trial Conduct.

docs.t: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton (W.D. Tenn.) — Courtroom technology
docs.x: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton, W.D. Tenn.. Courtroom technology: The courtroom has a document camera, monitors (counsel tables, witness box, bench, jury box), telephone conferencing, interpreter and hearing-assistance equipment, and laptop connections. Contact the court before the proceeding to test compatibility.

docs.x: Judge Charmiane G. Claxton, W.D. Tenn.. Social Security appeals and closing cases: The page posts a plaintiff’s fact sheet for Social Security appeals (application type and dates, vocational factors, basis of the ALJ’s decision, impairments, treating-physician opinions, and tables of testimony and medical evidence), with transcript citations required for each starred item. Civil cases are closed for statistical purposes after final judgment following a verdict, decision, or stipulation; this does not affect post-trial motions or fees and costs.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Rule 16(b) scheduling order (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Rule 16(b) scheduling order (trap): The judge’s form sets separate joinder and amendment deadlines for plaintiff and defendant, plus dates for each side’s Rule 26 expert disclosures, Rule 26(e) supplementation, written discovery, depositions, and dispositive motions. Absent good cause, the dates won’t be modified or extended. Motions to compel must be filed and served within 45 days of the default or of service of the response, answer, or objection at issue, unless extended for good cause; otherwise the objection to the default or response is waived. Final Rule 26(a)(3) witness and exhibit lists are due on set dates for each side, with a set number of days to object. The joint pretrial order, jury instructions, and motions in limine share a single due date, and the order fixes the pretrial conference and trial dates.

docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Court’s track scheduling forms: The page also posts the court’s Standard, Expedited, and Complex Track forms (for example, standard track: discovery closes 300 days after service on the first defendant; Daubert motions 15 days and dispositive motions 30 days after the close). They restate L.R. 7.2 (proposed orders to the judge’s ECF mailbox, consultation before non-Rule 12/56/59/60 motions, leave for other replies within 7 days) and allow a reply on Rule 12 and 56 motions within 14 days (L.R. 12.1(c), 56.1(c)).

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Voir dire
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Voir dire: The judge asks standard questions first (trial length, case knowledge, ties to counsel, parties, and witnesses, prior jury and litigation experience, ability to follow the law, disabilities), then lets counsel conduct additional voir dire before marking challenges. In criminal cases the court also asks about law-enforcement employment; jurors answering yes about criminal-matter involvement (or, in drug cases, drug experiences) come forward to discuss it at the bench with court and counsel.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Preliminary instructions
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Preliminary instructions: Jurors are told they may take notes, which stay in the jury room overnight. Openings are described as an outline, not evidence or argument; in criminal cases the defense may, but need not, open.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Standard civil charge
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Standard civil charge: The court’s civil charge covers general duties, preponderance, expert, deposition, and interrogatory evidence, note use, stipulations, compensatory, punitive (malicious, wanton, or oppressive conduct, assessed separately for each defendant, and only after unanimous actual or nominal damages), and nominal damages (a token sum such as $1.00, not combined with compensatory damages). A copy of the instructions goes to the jury room. The deliberation charge includes language encouraging a verdict and asking jurors in the minority to reconsider, without surrendering honest convictions.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Standard criminal charge
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Standard criminal charge: The criminal charge tracks the Sixth Circuit pattern numbering (e.g., 2.01A multiple counts, 7.02B defendant’s testimony, 7.03 expert testimony) and includes forms for judicial notice of venue, stipulations (including a prior-felony stipulation), law-enforcement witnesses, and the indictment. The verdict form goes to the jury in a folder that is returned to the marshal during breaks. Jury notes go through the marshal, and jurors must not disclose their numerical division.

Lead trial counsel must appear, and parties or corporate representatives with full authority to approve any settlement must be present in person, along with an insurer or indemnitor representative with authority to pay the full policy limits. Plaintiff must make a good-faith settlement proposal at least 14 days before the conference; defendant must make a good-faith counter-proposal at least 7 days before. At least 3 business days before, submit to ECF_Judge_Pham@tnwd.uscourts.gov an in camera statement covering the evidence and law, the relief sought (plaintiff itemizes damages; defendant lists mitigating factors), strengths and weaknesses, and settlement talks so far. Do not file it. Clear the entire day. The posted confidenti

docs.t: Judge Tu M. Pham (W.D. Tenn.) — Jury voir dire
docs.x: Judge Tu M. Pham, W.D. Tenn.. Jury voir dire: The court asks the whole panel 15 standard questions (case length, prior knowledge, acquaintance with parties, counsel, firms, and witnesses, prior lawsuits and claims, similar experiences, prior jury service, burden of proof, impartiality, and hardship). Each panel member then answers individual questions (name and age, residence, marital status, children, education, legal training, 10 years of employment for the juror and household adults, and hobbies). Attorneys then may ask additional questions.

docs.t: Judge Tu M. Pham (W.D. Tenn.) — Sample jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Tu M. Pham, W.D. Tenn.. Sample jury instructions: The page posts complete jury-instruction sets from past trials as samples: a standard set (Barnett), Title VII discrimination (Kumar), medical malpractice (Fabery and McDaniel), breach of contract and promissory fraud (Craftco), wrongful death and products liability (Vest), and personal injury (Lyons). The Fabery set cites T.P.I.–Civil pattern instructions.

docs.t: Judge Tu M. Pham (W.D. Tenn.) — Scheduling orders
docs.x: Judge Tu M. Pham, W.D. Tenn.. Scheduling orders: The page links the district’s Local Rule 16.2 Standard, Expedited, and Complex Track scheduling-order templates (identical on every judge’s page). They set motion-to-compel deadlines of 45 days after the default or response (30 days if it falls within 30 days of the discovery deadline), require a proposed order in word-processing format to the presiding judge’s ECF mailbox and consultation before most motions, and bar replies without leave except on Rule 12(b) and 56 motions.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Motions practice (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Motions practice (trap): Before filing any motion, meet and confer on its substance and state in the motion whether it is opposed (in a criminal case, also probation’s position where appropriate). Label joint, uncontested, and agreed motions as such in the title and body. The page limits in N.D. Ind. L.R. 7-1(e) are strictly enforced. Oral argument on civil motions is granted only in exceptional cases. Extension motions must state opposing counsel’s position and be filed as far ahead as possible; the court expects scheduling-order deadlines to be met. No off-the-record inquiries about when a substantive motion will be decided. Once a summary judgment motion has been fully briefed for 180 days, or any other motion for 90 days, counsel may file a status report on the motion’s effect on the parties and the case.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Filing order and citation format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Filing order and citation format (trap): File the motion and its exhibits before the supporting brief, so the brief can cite their docket numbers. Exhibits may be attached to the motion or filed separately (the motion first, with an appendix); a response, reply, or surreply with exhibits starts with an appendix of exhibits. Give each e-filed exhibit a number and a descriptive name (for example, “Ex. 1—Smith Dep.”), not just “Exhibit 1.” Cite the docket entry, attachment, and .pdf header page, as in “(ECF 42-8 at 5)”; for depositions add page and line, as in “(Johnson Dep. Tr. 10:4–13, ECF 38-2 at 3).” Hyperlinks to cited law are preferred but not required.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Summary judgment (trap): A party planning a summary judgment motion must first ask the other parties whether they also plan to file one. Cite specific evidence for every fact; unsupported facts may be disregarded. Statements of undisputed material facts and responses are filed separately from the briefs, with line, paragraph, or page cites. In complex cases an agreed timeline of events is helpful. Deposition cites need page and line, and the exhibit must include the cited pages plus at least three pages before and after; motions lacking the excerpts may be summarily denied. Cross-motions follow an automatic four-brief schedule (motion; cross-motion and response; reply and cross-response; cross-reply), using the CM/ECF events specified. Motions to strike are strongly disfavored; argue admissibility in the briefs, and if a motion to strike is truly warra

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Other motions
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Other motions: When a complaint is amended as of course after a Rule 12 motion, the court’s standard practice is to deny the pending Rule 12 motion as moot. Rule 702 motions are not motions in limine: file them by the scheduling-order deadline, with any summary judgment motion or no later than the dispositive motion deadline. TRO and preliminary injunction motions must address each Rule 65 requirement plus when the irreparable harm will occur, any discovery needed, whether an evidentiary or argument hearing is sought, and a proposed timeline. Criminal motions: both the local criminal and civil rules apply. Written motions are preferred over oral ones, and stipulated or agreed motions are appreciated.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Trial setting and continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Trial setting and continuances (trap): Civil trial dates are not set until the dispositive motion deadline has passed and dispositive and Rule 702 motions are decided. A motion to set trial earlier must state whether it is a jury trial, the expected length, proposed dates (at least 180 days after an unexpired dispositive deadline), and opposing counsel’s position. Trial scheduling conferences are by video; be ready to report on settlement, offer trial dates starting 6 months out, and flag trial issues. Pretrial deadlines, usually starting ten weeks before trial, come in the Order for Civil Trial, Final Pretrial Conference, and Order Controlling the Case. Criminal trial dates are usually set at arraignment. A motion to continue trial must include a speedy trial waiver signed by the defendant (by hand or electronically).

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Final pretrial conference and jury selection
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Final pretrial conference and jury selection: The final pretrial conference covers settlement or plea status, witnesses, exhibits and objections, motions in limine, deposition designations, stipulations, voir dire, time limits for openings and closings, witness separation, and daily schedules. Raise non-routine legal or evidentiary issues there after conferring. Counsel receive a link to juror questionnaires by noon on the Friday before trial (hard copies can be reviewed in the Clerk’s Office after noon that day). Refer to jurors only by number. Civil: usually eight jurors, no alternates, and at least three peremptories per side (exact number set at the final pretrial conference). Criminal: twelve jurors and two alternates, ordinarily 6 government and 10 defense peremptories plus one each for alternates. The court posts its standard criminal voir dire

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Courtroom conduct and objections (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Courtroom conduct and objections (trap): Stand when speaking and address the court, not opposing counsel. Openings, closings, and examinations are from the lectern; ask permission to leave it or approach a witness. Request that the court designate a witness as an expert after laying qualifications. No exhibit in opening without court approval unless admissibility is stipulated. A plaintiff suggesting a damages number must state it in the opening segment of closing, must reserve rebuttal time on the record, and must spend most of the time in the opening segment. Stand to object and state only the grounds; no further argument without permission. Only the lawyer who handled direct may object during other counsel’s examination of that witness, and only the lawyer who will cross may object during direct.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Depositions at trial
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Depositions at trial: Agreed deposition summaries are strongly urged, especially for any deposition over forty-five minutes, but are allowed only by stipulation. Edit transcripts and videos with opposing counsel to cut unnecessary material. Read-in testimony uses a person in the witness box reading the answers; the marked original transcript (and any video) is offered as an exhibit but not sent to the jury. Resolve objections made at the deposition before the final pretrial conference. Deposed treating physicians are presumed unavailable under Rule 32(a)(4); a written objection showing good cause must be filed at least 30 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Exhibits (trap): Mark exhibits with Clerk’s Office stickers before trial (plaintiff numbers, defendant letters; re-mark deposition exhibits), paginate every page, and staple multi-page exhibits unless in a tabbed binder. Prepare 4 tabbed exhibit binders (bench, courtroom deputy, witness stand, opposing counsel) plus an empty tabbed jury binder kept by the deputy and filled as exhibits are admitted; three-hole punch all exhibits in advance. Get leave of court before publishing admitted exhibits to the jury. Show demonstratives to opposing counsel before trial; only unopposed ones may be shown without leave. Arrange oversized exhibits with the deputy at least two weeks before trial, and substitute photographs for drugs, currency, firearms, and other dangerous items.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Jury instructions: The court prepares all standard opening, closing, and general instructions. Deadlines to confer and submit proposed instructions and verdict forms are set in the Order for Civil Trial or the criminal Discovery and Scheduling Order. Use the Seventh Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions first, then other circuits’ patterns and the Indiana patterns, and include points and authorities with each proposed instruction. Instructions are settled at a conference near the close of evidence, before closings.

docs.t: Judge Cristal C. Brisco (N.D. Ind.) — Trial logistics
docs.x: Judge Cristal C. Brisco, N.D. Ind.. Trial logistics: Trial days generally run 9:00 a.m. to about 5:00 p.m. Be in the courtroom 15 minutes early each day and 30 minutes early on day one, and give the deputy an updated witness list with phonetic spellings at the first-day attorney conference. Do not run out of witnesses. A witness both sides will call is usually examined fully in the plaintiff’s or government’s case-in-chief. Arrange daily or realtime transcripts with the court reporter at least two weeks before trial, and give the reporter a list of unusual terms and names. Coordinate equipment use and training with the deputy at the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Summary judgment (trap): Before filing any summary judgment motion, the parties must confer in good faith (by actually talking, not just by email or letter) to streamline issues, address choice of law, and plan the presentation; the motion must certify that they did. Failure to confer or certify may get the motion summarily denied or stricken. For anticipated cross-motions, propose a consolidated briefing schedule for approval before filing. File a separate appendix of evidence as the primary docket entry, with an index describing each exhibit (e.g., “Jane Doe’s Deposition . . . Exhibit 1”) and each exhibit as its own separately titled, text-searchable attachment; never attach exhibits to the motion, brief, or statement of material facts. A courtesy binder (double-sided) is encouraged for large records and may be ordered. Cite exhibits with particulari

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — “Speed bump” deadline (trap)
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. “Speed bump” deadline (trap): The court sets a “speed bump” 30 days before the close of discovery. It is the deadline for motions to extend discovery or continue other pretrial deadlines; after it passes, such motions are approved only for extraordinary reasons directed to the presiding judge, and good cause alone is not enough. File motions to compel and other schedule-affecting motions early enough to allow briefing and a ruling before the speed bump. Discovery motions filed during the speed-bump period or after discovery closes ordinarily go to Judge Leichty rather than the magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Motions, contact, and chambers copies
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Motions, contact, and chambers copies: Briefing schedules and page limits follow Local Rule 7.1 (as the page cites it). Courtesy hard copies are ordinarily unnecessary but are encouraged for complex filings. Status, scheduling, settlement, and other non-merits inquiries may go to the case manager or law clerks; never discuss the merits with staff. Copy all parties on any email to chambers.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Case management and trial setting
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Case management and trial setting: The magistrate judge holds the Rule 16(b) conference about 30 days after the last party appears; counsel must attend unless excused, and must come prepared to discuss summary judgment and narrowing of issues. The resulting scheduling order and Memorandum of Status Conference change only for good cause. Trial is set at a status conference about 30 days before discovery closes. Criminal trials take precedence; counsel wanting more certainty may consent to the magistrate judge (the judge does not see who declined consent). Private ADR is encouraged; a magistrate judge settlement conference is available in an appropriate case. Under the COVID-19 tab, status conferences are held by telephone.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Civil pretrial deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Civil pretrial deadlines (trap): At least 28 days before the final pretrial conference, exchange (not file) witness lists and deposition excerpts, exhibit lists and exhibits (not demonstratives), and contentions. At least 21 days before, exchange objections to witnesses, depositions, and exhibits, and proposed joint jury instructions. At least 14 days before, file evidentiary objections or motions to exclude experts (unless due sooner), plaintiff’s trial brief, proposed instructions, verdict forms, and voir dire questions (also emailed to chambers), the motion in limine, and the proposed final pretrial order. At least 7 days before, file opposing trial briefs, objections to instructions, verdict forms, and voir dire, and responses to motions in limine. The final pretrial conference is treated as the first day of trial; the final pretrial order will be

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Motions in limine and trial briefs
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Motions in limine and trial briefs: Only one motion in limine per party (with as many issues as needed), with supporting memoranda, at least 14 days before the final pretrial conference; responses at least 7 days before must state any part not opposed. Oral motions in limine only for good cause; rulings are interlocutory. Trial briefs are required unless excused and must cover issues, elements, stipulations, anticipated evidentiary and legal issues with authority, and each witness’s expected testimony.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Exhibits (trap): The parties must jointly prepare one set of exhibit binders and one flash drive (each exhibit a separate PDF) for the court, numbered (not lettered), with dividers; a joint exhibit list is preferred. Deliver to chambers by 5:00 p.m. the Wednesday before trial, and give each side’s exhibit list to the case manager by the same time. Demonstratives go to chambers with the other exhibits by the same Wednesday deadline; objections to them are due by noon the Thursday before trial. New or modified demonstratives are barred at trial absent good cause.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Civil jury selection and instructions
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Civil jury selection and instructions: The court conducts most voir dire and, in appropriate cases on request, allows a set time for attorney voir dire. Juror questionnaires may be reviewed at the clerk’s office the Friday before trial after 2:00 p.m.; if provided electronically, they may not be photographed or reproduced. The court gives Seventh Circuit civil instructions 1.01, 1.04, 1.06, 1.11-13, 1.27, and 1.32-34 in every case; parties must supply all substantive instructions. The instruction conference is on the record near the close of evidence, with a redline against the model instructions, and all instructions except those on deliberations are read before closing arguments.

docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Trial conduct
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Trial conduct: Trial days run 9:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Time limits on openings and closings are set after consulting counsel. Have enough witnesses to fill the day, and raise out-of-sequence professional witnesses with opposing counsel first. Ask permission to approach the witness or bench; the podium is optional (in criminal trials, wear a microphone if not at it), and stand when examining or addressing the court. Avoid first names, never address a juror by name, and follow the Seventh Circuit’s Standards for Professional Conduct. State routine objections briefly in open court; speaking objections will be cut off, only the examining attorney may object for that witness, and no colloquy between counsel. docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Criminal pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Criminal pretrial (trap): The magistrate judge handles initial appearance, arraignment, and detention, and usually enters the standard scheduling order, with trial generally 45 to 60 days from arraignment; a notice of complex case filed before arraignment gets a trial-setting hearing before Judge Leichty. Seek changes to the standard order by its modification deadline. docs.t: Judge Damon Ray Leichty (N.D. Ind.) — Criminal trial
docs.x: Judge Damon Ray Leichty, N.D. Ind.. Criminal trial: Proposed final instructions (with authorities) and verdict forms are due by noon ET the Wednesday the week before trial, in Word (not PDF) to leichty_chambers@innd.uscourts.gov and filed; proposed voir dire questions are due by noon ET that Thursday. The court circulates its own sets first, so do not duplicate them. The judge conducts voir dire and usually seats 12 jurors and 2 alternates from a 32-36 person venire; peremptories are taken one at a time at the bench, alternating between the defendant and the government. Questionnaires may be reviewed after 12:00 p.m. ET one business day before trial (the separate questionnaire tab says the Friday before trial after 2:00 p.m.). docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Motions and chambers copies
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Motions and chambers copies: Briefing schedules and page limits follow Local Rule 7-1. There are no motion days or motion calls. Extra chambers copies are ordinarily unnecessary, though the court may ask for a courtesy hard copy of a particularly lengthy filing. Discovery disputes are ordinarily referred to the assigned magistrate judge. Proposed orders go to the chambers mailbox.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Settlement and trial setting (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Settlement and trial setting (trap): Private ADR is encouraged; the court will refer a case to a magistrate judge for a settlement conference only on a showing that private ADR is inappropriate or has been tried without success. The court confers with counsel before setting trial, and criminal trials take precedence; certainty comes only on the eve of trial. The court urges consent to a magistrate judge for a firmer date. Report a civil settlement promptly to (219) 852-6637; jury costs may be assessed if the court is not told before the first day of trial. After a settlement report, the court usually denies pending motions as moot and gives 30 days to file dismissal papers.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Civil final pretrial and motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Civil final pretrial and motions in limine (trap): A final pretrial conference precedes every jury trial. File a proposed pretrial order following Rule 16(e), Appendix A of the Local Rules, and the “Scheduling, Pretrial Conference, and Trial Order” entered once trial is set, which also sets the other pretrial deadlines. Motions in limine are due at least 14 days before the final pretrial conference, and each side may file only one (with any number of points). Each point must show why the evidence might be offered, why it is inadmissible, and what harm an in-trial objection would cause. Requests must clearly identify the evidence to be excluded; motions aimed at broad categories are less likely to be granted. Orders in limine are interlocutory and only require the topic to be raised outside the jury’s hearing first.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Trial briefs (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Trial briefs (trap): All parties must file trial briefs identifying the issues, the elements of each claim, stipulations, anticipated evidentiary and legal issues with authority, and each witness’s anticipated testimony. Plaintiff’s brief is due at least 21 days before the final pretrial conference, the opposing party’s at least 14 days before, and any supplementary brief at least 7 business days before.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Civil jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Civil jury instructions: Proposed instructions, citing the source or authority for each, are due at least 21 days before the final pretrial conference: file them and also email them in Word to lund_chambers@innd.uscourts.gov. Confer beforehand to cut down the number of proposals. The court routinely gives Seventh Circuit Civil Instructions 1.01, 1.04, 1.06–1.08, 1.11–1.13, 1.16–1.18, 1.27, and 1.32–1.34; the parties supply all substantive instructions. Written objections to others’ proposals are due at least 14 days before the final pretrial conference. Instructions are settled on the record near the close of the evidence. Unless asked otherwise, the court gives all but the closing instructions before final arguments, and the jury gets a written copy.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Civil jury selection
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Civil jury selection: Juror questionnaires may be viewed in the Clerk’s Office after 2:00 p.m. the day before trial; copies and a random list are given the morning of trial. Eight jurors, no alternates; counsel will be asked to agree that a verdict of at least six jurors is valid under Rule 48. The court conducts voir dire and invites additional questions at sidebar. Each side has three peremptories, exercised one at a time, alternating from plaintiff; there are no backstrikes.

docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Depositions at trial: The court urges agreed summaries of any deposition that would take more than thirty minutes to read or play, and expects video depositions to be edited for dead time and repetition. Played or read depositions are presumed not to be reported; give the deputy a transcript and a list of the portions used. In bench trials, the judge prefers to read the depositions personally.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Criminal pretrial and pleas
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Criminal pretrial and pleas: The magistrate judge handles the initial appearance, arraignment, and detention and enters a scheduling order setting trial within the 70-day speedy trial clock; Judge Lund then enters a supplemental order controlling the trial. Non-dispositive motions go to the magistrate judge, including motions to continue trial (state the length requested). Motions in limine, motions to suppress, and motions to continue sentencing go to Judge Lund. A discovery request beyond the standard discovery order must explain why that order is inadequate. After a plea agreement or notice of intent to plead is filed, the deputy schedules a change of plea hearing; if the judge is unavailable, the magistrate judge may take the plea with the parties’ consent.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Criminal final pretrial conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Criminal final pretrial conference (trap): Usually about 10 days before trial. Each defendant must attend unless excused in advance, and a request to excuse must be made by motion or in the pretrial statement at least 4 days before the conference. File a pretrial statement addressing stipulations, exhibits and admissibility, experts, and the other matters in the standard scheduling order. The conference also covers motions in limine, preliminary rulings on co-conspirator statements, and Rule 404(b) proffers.

docs.t: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund (N.D. Ind.) — Criminal jury instructions and selection
docs.x: Judge Gretchen Suzanne Lund, N.D. Ind.. Criminal jury instructions and selection: The court files its proposed final instructions and proposed voir dire questions first. Proposed voir dire questions must be filed, and a witness list sent to chambers, at least three business days before trial. Twelve jurors and two alternates for trials of two weeks or less; defense has 10 and the government 6 peremptories, plus one per side for every two alternates. Questionnaires are viewable after 2:00 p.m. one business day before trial; strikes alternate with the defense first, and there are no backstrikes.

docs.t: Judge Holly Ann Brady (N.D. Ind.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge Holly Ann Brady, N.D. Ind.. Motions and hearings: Briefing schedules and page limits follow Local Rule 7.1 (as the page cites it). There are no motion days or motion calls; request oral argument by motion, and note that setting argument may delay the ruling. Courtesy copies are ordinarily unnecessary, though the court may request one for a particularly lengthy submission. Counsel may attend some proceedings by telephone on request and court order.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Proposed orders, exhibits, and citations
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Proposed orders, exhibits, and citations: A proposed order must accompany every motion, with “[PROPOSED]” in the caption (superseding ECF Manual § 2(h)). Email it in Word to efile_ohta@casd.uscourts.gov with the case number and name in the subject line; never file it on the docket. Excerpt exhibits to relevant material and label, date, tab, and index them. Don’t attach documents already on any federal district court docket; cite them by case name, docket number, filing date, and pin. Give Westlaw or Lexis cites for unreported cases, and attach copies of cases unavailable there. Parties seeking or opposing substantially the same relief must coordinate and consolidate briefing; notices of joinder are allowed.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Ex parte, TROs, and continuances
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Ex parte, TROs, and continuances: Meet and confer before any ex parte motion and attach a declaration on the efforts to contact, the good-faith efforts, and opposing counsel’s position. Serve by email or overnight mail. Unopposed within 2 court days, it may be granted on that ground; decided without a hearing unless the court sets argument. TRO motions must be briefed and are heard ex parte only in extraordinary circumstances. To continue any date, meet and confer first; if agreed, file a joint motion with a declaration of reasons and email a Word proposed order stating the current and new dates. If not agreed, file an ex parte motion at least 2 court days before the event or deadline.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Sealing: Sealing is strongly discouraged; agreement of the parties or a protective-order designation is not enough. Motions must be narrowly tailored and state the legal standard, the interests warranting sealing, the injury if denied, and why less restrictive alternatives won’t do, with declarations as needed. Attach a highlighted unredacted version marked “FILED UNDER SEAL,” file a public redacted version (or a slip sheet if sealing in full), and submit a proposed order listing in a table each document or portion to be sealed. Sealing entire pleadings or briefs is granted only in extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Settlement: Notify the court and the magistrate judge immediately. Unless a Rule 41(a)(1) notice of dismissal is filed, file a joint motion to dismiss and email the proposed order within 28 days of settlement.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Civil pretrial and motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Civil pretrial and motions in limine (trap): Email the proposed pretrial order, complying with Civil Local Rule 16.1(f)(6)(c), to efile_ohta@casd.uscourts.gov at least 7 days before the pretrial conference. Motions in limine are for evidentiary issues only; Daubert, judgment on the pleadings, summary judgment, leave to amend, and bifurcation motions are not proper in limine motions. Meet and confer first and file a declaration (date, efforts, positions). Five motions per side, motions and responses up to 5 pages, no replies. Exchange and email Final Exhibit and Witness Lists 14 days before trial. Deliver one courtesy copy of trial exhibits (arranged with the deputy) and an electronic copy (e.g., USB drive) at least 3 days before trial. Exhibits are numbered only, not lettered.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Jury instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Headings show “Jointly Proposed” or the proposing party; cite the source beneath each heading; prefer Ninth Circuit or CACI (criminal: California Criminal) models. Color code: model text black, stipulated modifications red (redline and strikethrough), plaintiff’s or the government’s edits blue, defendant’s green. Competing versions go back to back, with each party’s factual or legal basis.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Trial: Civil trials generally run 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., Monday through Thursday, under a court-set overall time limit (excluding jury selection). Criminal trials run Monday to Thursday, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. the first day and 8:30 to 3:30 after. The court conducts voir dire (about 32 prospective jurors in civil cases); no questionnaires without authorization, and attorney follow-up only if permitted. In criminal cases, cause and alternating peremptory challenges are exercised outside the panel’s presence. Stay out of the well except in voir dire, openings, and closings; examine from the podium and ask before approaching a witness; one lawyer per witness; no speaking objections. Sidebars are disfavored in criminal trials.

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Criminal: continuances and sentencing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. Late motions require an in-person request at the hearing; email the proposed order. Ask to continue a sentencing no later than noon on the Thursday before the following week’s sentencing. File a sentencing summary chart, and any memorandum, at least 7 days before sentencing (holidays excluded); no more than five sentencing letters without leave. Late filings may mean a continuance at minimum and repeated lateness possible fines. Rule 11 pleas before the magistrate judge are encouraged. The court prefers a presentence

docs.t: Judge Jinsook Ohta (S.D. Cal.) — Criminal: pretrial deadlines
docs.x: Judge Jinsook Ohta, S.D. Cal.. docs.x: Judge Linda Lopez, S.D. Cal.. docs.t: Judge Linda Lopez (S.D. Cal.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Linda Lopez, S.D. Cal.. No later than 15 days before the dispositive-motion deadline, all parties on the same side must meet and confer about whether and on what bases they will move. Cross-motions share the motion deadline; coordinate briefing or file declarations explaining why not, or the court may strike the briefs and require a joint motion. Memoranda must cite the separate statement by fact number, or specific record pages.

docs.x: Judge M. James Lorenz, S.D. Cal.. docs.t: Judge M. James Lorenz (S.D. Cal.) — Civil pretrial and trial

docs.x: Judge M. James Lorenz, S.D. Cal.. docs.t: Judge M. James Lorenz (S.D. Cal.) — Sentencing (trap)

docs.x: Judge Amanda K. Brailsford, D. Idaho. Motions and hearings: The court issues the notice of hearing; you do not need to call to schedule one (L.R. 7.1). Before filing an Iqbal/Twombly motion to dismiss, contact opposing counsel, point out the pleading’s shortcomings, and try to agree on an amended complaint; the motion must state that this was done and that the motion is still necessary. The court may set a hearing or briefing schedule on its own. If a motion would benefit from briefing, jointly email the deputy a proposed briefing schedule within 2 business days of filing. docs.t: Judge Andrea Wood (N.D. Ill.) — Hearings and contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. Hearings and contacting chambers: Most status hearings are by telephone; the call sheet and the docket entry say whether a hearing is by phone or in person. No speakerphones, a landline is preferred, stay muted except when speaking, and call from a quiet place (not a vehicle, outdoors, or a public area). Recording or rebroadcasting is prohibited. Direct all case-related inquiries (scheduling, motion status, trial logistics) jointly to the courtroom deputy. Do not communicate with the court about the merits by letter, phone, or email; requests for relief must be by motion, brief, or status report served on opposing counsel.

docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. Courtesy copies and filing: No courtesy copies unless the court directs; ordered copies go to the drop-box outside the deputy’s office (Room 2140). docs.t: Judge Andrea Wood (N.D. Ill.) — Proposed orders and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. Proposed orders and extensions (trap): No proposed orders for routine motions (such as extensions) or dispositive motions. Never file a proposed order as a stand-alone docket entry, even an agreed or stipulated protective order; file a motion to enter it and simultaneously email the proposed order in Word-compatible format to Proposed_Order_Wood@ilnd.uscourts.gov (subject: case number and name, motion docket number, and order title), serving all parties. Before seeking an extension, contact all parties; the motion must say whether it is the first or a later request, give reasons and prior relief granted, and state whether anyone objects.

docs.t: Judge Andrea Wood (N.D. Ill.) — Discovery motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. Discovery motions (trap): Discovery motions are discouraged and won’t be heard without L.R. 37.2 compliance, stated with specificity in the motion. Meet and confer face to face or by phone; exchanging letters normally isn’t enough. Be prepared to argue on presentment; the court often rules after argument without briefing or sets expedited briefing. Notify the court immediately if a discovery motion is withdrawn. Before moving to compel over voluminous electronic records, confer with an IT representative of the storage facility, with the requesting party’s IT specialist present. There is no required order of discovery, and a pending dispositive motion does not by itself stay discovery unless applicable law provides.

docs.t: Judge Andrea Wood (N.D. Ill.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. Summary judgment (trap): Movant is limited to 80 statements of undisputed material fact and respondent to 40 without prior leave. File 56.1 statements and responses separately from the memoranda, with line, paragraph, or page citations; noncompliance can mean stricken briefs, disregarded or admitted facts, and denial. In complex cases the court may ask for a timeline.

docs.t: Judge Andrea Wood (N.D. Ill.) — Status reports
docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. Status reports: New civil cases usually get an initial status hearing about 60 days after filing. After a Rule 26(f) conference, file a joint initial status report, 5 pages maximum, at least 7 calendar days before the hearing, following the template (including citizenship of each party and of LLC or partnership members where diversity or supplemental jurisdiction is involved, ESI, Rule 502(d), and proposed limits changes). Do not give settlement figures or say which parties declined magistrate consent. In a reassigned case, existing dates stay in effect; file a joint reassignment status report, 5 pages maximum, within 14 days of the reassignment order (by plaintiff’s counsel if no defense appearance), covering discovery status, pending motions, prior rulings, trial readiness, and referrals.

Include jurisdiction (explaining any amount in controversy and any dispute), trial attorneys, an agreed case statement, will-call, may-call, and deposition witness lists with 2–3 sentence role descriptions, page-and-line deposition designation charts with objections and responses, an exhibit chart with objections (e.g., Rule 402, 403) and bases for admissibility, and itemized damages with the evidentiary basis for each. Unobjected exhibits come in without foundation, but in jury trials an exhibit not referenced or published before the close of evidence is not in evidence unless ordered. Two binders of objected-to exhibits are due at least 5 business days before the final pretrial conference; 3 sets of final binders

docs.x: Judge Andrea Wood, N.D. Ill.. docs.t: Judge April Perry (N.D. Ill.) — Briefs, pleadings, and motions to dismiss
docs.x: Judge April Perry, N.D. Ill.. Briefs, pleadings, and motions to dismiss: Opening and response briefs 15 pages, replies 10, unless ordered otherwise; follow L.R. 5.2 and file searchable OCR PDFs. Amended complaints must attach a redline against the prior version (not required of pro se litigants). When a motion to dismiss is filed, consider amending under Rule 15(a)(1)(B). If you amend, the movant answers or renews within 21 days; if not, respond within 21 days and reply within 10 days. The response must address whether the deficiencies are curable, and if the motion is litigated and granted, dismissal may be with prejudice. For conferences before Judge Perry, exchange demand and offer letters in advance and, if no deal, email them to the proposed-order inbox (not the docket). Nothing is filed under seal without a prior order identifying the document. The motion must describe each document, explain why confidentiality is necessary with authority, and address relevance. HIPAA qualified protective orders must bar use outside the litigation and require return or destruction of health information at the end.

Do not submit one for extensions, page-limit expansions, discovery motions, or appearances unless asked. docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Discovery (trap): No discovery motion will be heard unless the movant complied with Local Rule 37.2 and states specifically when and how. Meet and confer face to face or by telephone; letters ordinarily are not enough. Briefing is rare: the motion is usually argued at a status or a separately set hearing, so come fully prepared. Any briefing will be expedited. There is no required sequence of discovery, and a pending motion (such as a motion to dismiss) does not stay discovery unless the court orders it.

docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Protective orders and sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Protective orders and sealing (trap): The judge will not sign a protective order that lets counsel decide what is confidential; it must list specific categories, and the motion must explain why each needs protection. No order may allow sealed filing just because material is designated confidential. Each sealing request needs a motion, filed and noticed before the filing’s due date, showing good cause. A protective order is not a binding good-cause finding if later challenged. Where sealing is allowed, file the entire unredacted filing (with all exhibits) under seal and a redacted version publicly.

Motions to strike all or part of a Local Rule 56.1 submission are disfavored; make objections to inadmissible or improper material in the response or reply brief.

Unlisted witnesses and exhibits are excluded, and objections not stated in the order are waived, absent good cause. docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Motions in limine (trap): Due 14 days before the final pretrial conference; responses 7 days before; not bound with the pretrial order. Limit: 15 pages total per side for motions and 15 for responses, absent leave; requests may be combined in one filing. docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Jury instructions and selection
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Jury instructions and selection: Use Seventh Circuit pattern instructions where they apply and Illinois Pattern Instructions for elements of Illinois claims. Agreed instructions are marked and numbered consecutively; disputed ones are numbered, name the proponent, and cite authority, with written objections citing authority. The judge uses a written juror questionnaire (samples are posted); propose only case-specific questions. The venire is about 24 people in civil cases and about 38 in single-defendant criminal cases; the court rules on cause challenges first, then peremptories alternate at sidebar, starting with plaintiff or the prosecution. Civil juries are typically twelve, all deliberating; criminal cases add one or two alternates.

docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Trial: Trial days typically run 10 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. with about an hour for lunch. The final pretrial conference is about 1–2 weeks before trial; lead trial counsel with full authority must attend. Exhibits are shown on the courtroom’s evidence presentation system (jurors have individual screens), but keep a hard copy set ready for deliberations. Deliver a bench book of exhibits at or before trial unless excused. Learn the JERS system before the final pretrial conference. Request daily or expedited transcripts from the court reporter at least 7 days before trial.

docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. If unsettled, deliver copies to chambers (not filed) at least 2 days before. Parties with full authority (including insurers) must attend in person; phone availability is not acceptable except in the most extenuating circumstances. Under the judge’s standing order, search or seizure warrants in a criminal case assigned to the judge go to Judge Kennelly, not the duty, designated, or emergency magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard (N.D. Ill.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard, N.D. Ill.. Trial (trap): Trial runs 9 a.m. to noon and 1:15 to 5 p.m., with one 15–20 minute recess each session.
